title: Discount Rate
subtitle: The discount rate reflects risk and opportunity cost
openingQuestion: When evaluating a high-risk project, do you use a high or low discount rate?
openingOptions: High - reflecting higher risk requires a higher expected return
Low - to make the value higher
Equal to the bank savings rate
explanation: The discount rate is the minimum return you require to accept the risk of an investment - it is an opportunity cost, not a technical parameter. The higher the risk, the higher that requirement, the stronger the discount, and the lower the present value. Because it sits in the denominator and is raised to a power over time, a small change in this rate shifts a valuation enormously - that's why every DCF model must come with a sensitivity table.

realWorldExample.company: Valuing a renewable-energy project vs a tech startup
realWorldExample.description: A solar power project with stable, predictable cash flow usually uses a lower discount rate (8-10%) than a tech startup with uncertain cash flow (discount rate 20-30%) - reflecting the different risk levels of the expected cash flows.

quiz.question: What is the discount rate in DCF valuation usually?
options: The average revenue growth rate of the last three years
The 12-month bank deposit interest rate
The central bank's target inflation rate
WACC, the business's weighted average cost of capital
quiz.explanation: In DCF, WACC is used as the discount rate because it reflects the real cost of capital (both equity and debt). A small change in WACC can produce a large change in valuation.

quiz.question: Two projects have the same expected future cash flow, but one is assessed as much riskier. What happens when the appropriate discount rate is applied to each?
options: The riskier project gets a higher discount rate so its NPV is lower
The two projects give equal NPV since expected cash flow is the same
The riskier project has higher NPV to compensate for that risk
They can't be compared since risk only affects cash flow, not r
quiz.explanation: This is how the discount rate 'penalizes' risk quantitatively: with the same expected cash flow, a riskier project must bear a higher discount rate, leading to a lower NPV - consistent with the intuition that an uncertain cash flow is worth less than a certain one.

quiz.question: What is the discount rate made up of?
options: The bank lending rate plus the corporate tax rate
The risk-free opportunity cost plus a risk premium
The inflation rate plus the business's growth rate
The cost of equity minus the tax shield from debt
quiz.explanation: The base is the return achievable while bearing almost no risk; the additional part is the price of uncertainty. The harder a cash flow is to predict, the larger the premium, and the smaller the present value.

quiz.question: Raising the discount rate from 10% to 12% affects which part of a DCF model the most?
options: The initial capital expenditure already spent at the present time
The cash flow of the first two years in the forecast period
The cash flow of the farthest years and the Terminal Value
The forecast revenue for the entire modeled period
quiz.explanation: The denominator (1+r)^n grows exponentially, so the farther out a cash flow is, the deeper the cut. Terminal Value usually makes up 60-80% of a model's value and sits at exactly the farthest point - that's why a few percentage points of r are enough to flip a conclusion.

quiz.question: Why is using the same discount rate for every project in a company wrong?
options: Because projects have completely different payback periods
Because WACC changes every quarter with market fluctuations
Because a larger project needs a higher discount rate than a small one
Because each project carries its own level of risk, not an average one
quiz.explanation: Using a company-wide WACC for everything unfairly penalizes safe projects and favors risky ones - over the years, the company ends up funneling capital into exactly the projects it should have rejected.

keyTakeaways: Discount rate = opportunity cost + risk premium
Higher risk → higher discount rate → lower PV
In DCF: WACC is usually used as the discount rate

practicePrompt.question: When valuing a high-risk startup, an investor uses a discount rate of 25%/year; when valuing an almost risk-free government bond, they use a discount rate of only 5%/year. Why is the gap between these two discount rates so large?
options: Discount rate = opportunity cost + a risk premium, so a startup's rate sits well above a bond's
The discount rate must always be identical across every asset type to ensure a fair comparison
The discount rate only depends on the central bank's interest rate, having nothing to do with any specific asset's risk
A startup always uses a lower discount rate because its growth potential compensates for its risk
practicePrompt.explanation: Discount rate = opportunity cost + risk premium. A riskier asset (like a startup) needs a larger risk premium to compensate for the possibility of losing capital, so its discount rate is much higher than an almost-safe asset (a government bond) - a higher discount rate also makes the present value (PV) of future cash flow lower.

summary.keyIdea: Discount rate = opportunity cost + risk premium
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Higher risk → higher discount rate → lower PV

application.title: Choose your own discount rate
application.message: Think of 2 investments you know - one safe (a savings deposit), one riskier (a stock) - and set a reasonable discount rate for each, explaining why they differ.
application.secondary: There's no fixed formula for the discount rate - this is an exercise in building intuition about risk.

sections.text: The discount rate isn't an arbitrary number - it's the minimum return an investor requires to accept the risk of a specific cash flow. The discount rate is exactly the bridge connecting risk to valuation: the higher the risk, the higher the discount rate, and the lower the PV of the same cash flow.
Where does the discount rate come from?

In essence, discount rate = opportunity cost (what an investor could earn from another investment of the same risk level) plus a matching risk premium. In business valuation via DCF, the standard discount rate is WACC - because it accurately reflects the true cost of both the debt and equity capital a business uses.
Example: renewable energy and a tech startup

A solar power project with a long-term electricity purchase contract has very predictable cash flow - the discount rate is usually just 8-10%. A tech startup without stable revenue yet has extremely uncertain cash flow - the discount rate can reach 20-30%. Suppose both expect to receive 100 million dong after 5 years: the energy project's PV = 100/(1.09)^5 ≈ 65 million dong; the startup's PV = 100/(1.25)^5 ≈ 33 million dong - the same future amount, but present values almost twice apart, purely because of different risk levels.

items: A high discount rate 'penalizes' uncertain cash flow - correctly reflecting our intuition about risk
In corporate DCF: use WACC; for an individual project with risk different from the company's, a separate adjustment may be needed
Being off by even a few percentage points in the discount rate can throw off a valuation significantly, especially with distant cash flows (terminal value)
The discount rate isn't fixed - it changes with market interest rates, risk appetite, and industry characteristics

lines: The discount rate is where risk gets turned into a number - learning to choose it correctly matters just as much as learning to calculate PV.
